Section A · Reflection

Learning reflections

Notes on organising the portfolio and learning to publish work online.

01

Markdown and Portfolio Structure

situation

I needed to organise professional and academic information into a portfolio that could be accessed online.

task

Present my background clearly and make project evidence easy for a reviewer to find.

action

I organised the content into sections, used headings and links, and connected the portfolio to my GitHub profile and project evidence.

result

The structure makes the relationship between my skills, projects and learning easier to follow. I still need to verify every link and attach the final supporting artefacts.

02

GitHub Pages

situation

A portfolio is more useful when a lecturer or employer can open it without downloading the source files.

task

Publish a clear online view of my work and keep the page navigable on desktop and mobile.

action

I use GitHub Pages to host my portfolio and organise the material with navigation links and distinct sections.

result

The online portfolio can serve as a single entry point for my PRP370S evidence. I should test the published links after each update.

03

Building my CV

situation

Applying for Work Integrated Learning means competing against many third-year students with similar qualifications, and my early CV was a plain list of subjects and jobs.

task

Produce a CV that shows an employer what I can actually build, and keep it honest and easy to scan in under a minute.

action

I restructured it around evidence: the enrolment system, the launched real-estate prototype and the AWS deployment, plus concrete tools (Java, Laravel, RESTful APIs, Cognito) instead of vague claims, and kept a one-page format.

result

The CV now doubles as my portfolio anchor — the same projects appear here on the site, in my GitHub repo and in interviews, so everything I claim can be checked in one click.

Section A · Agile evidence reflection

Working with Agile Evidence

Working with the Sentiment Mood Detector project helps connect planning with software work. A team charter clarifies shared expectations, user stories explain value from a user’s perspective, and a prioritised backlog makes the next tasks visible. Acceptance criteria help the team understand what to check; dated logbook entries and board updates can make progress and decisions easier to trace. I will use the available evidence to reflect honestly on what I learned and contributed.

This is a learning reflection, separate from the Section B project reflections and team evidence.

Group 3D · PRP372S

Writing the charter as a team

Our group of four had to deliver a sentiment analysis web app in two sprints mapped across eight project weeks, with a heavy academic workload, no budget and uneven skill levels. The charter records our mission, success definition, roles, ceremonies, communication rules, Definition of Done, values, risks and milestones.

Charter highlights
  • Agile framework with a product backlog and a logbook
  • Daily stand-ups, weekly planning, review/demo and retrospectives
  • Response times: 1–2 hours in core hours, 30 minutes for urgent messages
  • Consensus first; majority vote when stuck, lecturer as escalation path
  • Definition of Done: tested, documented, approved, deployed, no critical bugs
  • Values: respect, transparency, accountability, trust, learning and collaboration

Backlog

User stories

What the team is building, written from the user’s point of view — each story carries acceptance criteria.

US-01User need

As a student, I want to paste a comment and instantly see whether its mood is positive, negative or neutral, so that I don't have to re-read feedback twice.

Acceptance criteria
Result appears without leaving the page
Mood is labelled with a confidence score
US-02User need

As a small business owner, I want to a confidence score with each result, so that I know how much to trust the reading.

Acceptance criteria
Score shown as a percentage
Low-signal comments read as neutral
US-03User need

As a social media user, I want to a mood summary of all my saved comments, so that I can see the overall tone of my feedback at a glance.

Acceptance criteria
Summary chart counts positive / negative / neutral
Chart updates as new comments are saved
US-04User need

As a returning user, I want to my past comments saved in a history, so that I can track results over time.

Acceptance criteria
Each saved entry shows its mood and score
History is stored in a database
US-05User need

As a first-time user, I want to a simple, easy-to-use interface, so that I can use the app without any training.

Acceptance criteria
One clear input and one clear result
No more than three steps to a result

Section B · Reflection

Project reflections

Honest STAR reflections on parts of the Sentiment Mood Detector project.

01

Running the sprints

situation

Two sprints across eight project weeks, with four members balancing other modules, meant tasks slipped early and stand-ups drifted.

task

Get the sprint rhythm working so the board told the truth about our progress.

action

We tightened stand-ups to three questions each, moved unfinished cards back to the backlog honestly, and the Agile Lead started each week by re-prioritising the backlog.

result

By sprint 2 every card on the board matched reality, milestones landed in their weeks, and the retrospective could focus on improvement instead of excuses.

02

Designing the comment experience

situation

Early wireframes crammed the input form, result and history onto one dense screen, and testers hesitated about what to do first.

task

Design a flow a first-time user can complete without instructions.

action

I cut the flow to three steps — type a comment, see the mood with its confidence, browse history — added plain-language labels and colour-coded results, and tested the flow with classmates before coding.

result

Test users completed the flow unaided on the first try, and the three-step pattern became the structure of the screens I built.

03

Testing the detector

situation

The first version of the detection logic misread short comments and missed flipped meanings like ‘not good’.

task

Make the mood labels trustworthy enough to show with a confidence score.

action

We built a test set of positive, negative, neutral and mixed comments, handled negation and intensifiers in the logic, and recorded every wrong result in a bug log for the tester to re-check.

result

Labels became stable on the test set, and showing a confidence score made even edge-case results feel honest instead of wrong.
